The miniature operas, each lasting under five minutes, were performed by students from the Royal College of Music and were based on themes of sustainability and innovation. Scientific demos ranged from quantum computing models to live displays of nanotechnology, while the “24/7” lecture segment featured experts from fields such as astrophysics, bioengineering, and artificial intelligence, providing audiences with round‑the‑clock access to current research discussions.

The event drew over 3,000 attendees, including scholars, industry leaders, and media representatives. By integrating performance art with scientific exposition, the ceremony underscored the organizers’ commitment to fostering a broader public understanding of science while celebrating artistic creativity. The award’s next iteration is slated for the following year, with plans to expand the program to include interactive workshops and a virtual reality exhibit.
author: Ars Technica

title: Google Launches WeatherNext 3 AI Weather Model
content:
Google has unveiled WeatherNext 3, its newest deep‑learning‑based meteorology platform that promises to reshape how weather data is generated and distributed. The company describes the system as the latest wave in a broader “sea change” in forecasting, following earlier iterations that have progressively incorporated neural networks to model atmospheric dynamics more accurately.

According to Google, WeatherNext 3 will feed directly into the weather information that appears in Google Search results, Google Maps, and the Gemini conversational AI. The integration aims to deliver more precise, real‑time forecasts to users across its services, leveraging the platform’s advanced algorithms to process vast amounts of meteorological data and produce localized predictions. The move follows the company’s broader strategy of embedding AI into everyday tools to enhance user experience.

While Google has not yet released detailed performance metrics, the announcement signals a continued push toward AI‑driven forecasting. If the projected improvements materialize, users could benefit from more reliable weather updates in navigation, travel planning, and daily decision‑making, reflecting the growing role of deep learning in climate science and consumer technology.
author: TechCrunch

title: Google Adds AI Voice Search to Gmail, Docs, and Keep
content:
A new conversational search feature has been rolled out, enabling users to locate both emails and draft documents through natural‑language queries. The update is part of the platform’s ongoing effort to streamline information retrieval, allowing users to ask questions such as “Show me the latest draft of the Q3 budget report” or “Find the email from Sarah about the client meeting.” The system interprets the query, pulls relevant items from the user’s mailbox and document repository, and presents them in a concise, searchable list.

Developers say the feature leverages the platform’s existing AI engine to parse intent, filter by metadata, and surface results that match the user’s request. It supports a range of filters—date ranges, senders, document types—and can even suggest related items that the user might have missed. Early adopters report that the conversational interface reduces the time spent navigating folders and improves accuracy when searching for specific content.

The update is available to all users immediately and is expected to enhance productivity across teams that rely on the platform for both email communication and document collaboration.
author: TechCrunch

title: Ollie Aims to Win AI Assistant Race with Privacy Focus
content:
A new family‑focused AI assistant has announced that it will collect detailed information about users’ daily routines, household schedules, and personal preferences. The company behind the product, which markets the assistant as a tool for simplifying family life, has stated that the data will not be used to train its own AI models or shared with third parties. The announcement comes amid growing scrutiny over how consumer data is handled by emerging AI services.

The assistant is designed to integrate with smart home devices, calendars, and messaging apps, gathering data such as meal plans, school schedules, and even bedtime rituals. According to the company’s privacy statement, the information will be stored locally on the device and only transmitted to the assistant’s servers when a user explicitly requests a service, such as setting a reminder or ordering groceries. The firm emphasized that its data‑processing pipeline excludes the use of personal data for model improvement and that no user data will be sold or disclosed to external entities.

Regulators and privacy advocates are watching the rollout closely. While the company’s assurances may address some concerns, critics point out that the lack of independent audits and the potential for future policy changes could undermine user trust. As the assistant moves toward commercial release, its approach to data handling will likely influence broader industry standards for privacy‑preserving AI services.
author: TechCrunch

title: Circular Launches Ring 3 Series with Contactless Payments and Vibration Alerts
content:
Circular Ring has unveiled its new Circular Ring 3 series, adding a fresh line to the growing portfolio of wearable health trackers. The announcement details a range of upgraded sensors, a slimmer design, and extended battery life, positioning the brand to compete in a market that has seen rapid innovation over the past year.

The launch follows the release of the Oura Ring 5 and RingConn Gen 3, both of which introduced advanced sleep‑tracking algorithms and improved connectivity. These developments have intensified competition among manufacturers, prompting a wave of product enhancements aimed at differentiating features such as biometric accuracy, user interface, and form factor.

With the Circular Ring 3 series now available, the company seeks to capture a share of the expanding smart‑ring segment. The new models are expected to appeal to consumers seeking a balance of performance and style, potentially reshaping market dynamics as brands continue to push the limits of wearable health technology.
author: TechCrunch

title: Qualcomm invests $70M in Ultrahuman for smart ring development
content:
Ultrahuman, the health‑tech startup known for its fitness app and wearable ecosystem, has announced a new milestone: it aims to reach a $200 million annual revenue run rate by January 2027. The company says the target will be driven in part by the launch of a Qualcomm‑powered smart ring, slated for release later this year. The ring will integrate advanced biometric sensors and a low‑power Snapdragon Wear 4100 platform, enabling continuous heart‑rate, sleep, and activity monitoring while maintaining a sleek, discreet form factor.

The move follows Ultrahuman’s recent expansion of its subscription services and hardware portfolio, which already includes a fitness app, a smart water bottle, and a line of smart clothing. By leveraging Qualcomm’s chip technology, the company hopes to differentiate its ring in a crowded wearable market and attract both health‑conscious consumers and professional athletes. If the product gains traction, the projected revenue run rate would place Ultrahuman among the leading players in the personal wellness sector, positioning it for further investment and potential strategic partnerships in the coming years.
author: TechCrunch

title: Nvidia to acquire Hugging Face for $12.9 billion
content:
Nvidia has entered into a deal that transfers control of a leading open‑source artificial‑intelligence platform and its associated developer community to the chipmaker. The agreement, announced earlier this week, places the widely used software framework under Nvidia’s direct oversight, granting the company influence over its future development roadmap and integration with Nvidia’s hardware portfolio.

Industry observers note that the acquisition expands Nvidia’s reach within the AI ecosystem, aligning a prominent open‑source resource with the firm’s GPU and accelerated computing offerings. By overseeing the platform and its community, Nvidia aims to streamline toolchains for AI researchers and developers, potentially accelerating the deployment of new models and applications across its hardware infrastructure.
author: BBC Technology

title: Chile fits injured Humboldt penguins with protective recovery vests
content:
In coastal regions of Chile, wildlife rehabilitators have begun fitting injured Humboldt penguins with specially designed recovery vests. The garments are intended to shield open wounds and surgical stitches from the birds’ own movements and the abrasive marine environment, thereby reducing the risk of infection and promoting more efficient healing.

The vests, made from lightweight, water‑resistant material, are tailored to each bird’s size and secured with adjustable fastenings that allow the penguins to swim and preen without compromising wound protection. Veterinarians overseeing the program report that the devices have already lowered the incidence of post‑operative complications, enabling a higher rate of successful releases back into the wild. Continued monitoring will assess long‑term outcomes, but early results suggest the vest system could become a standard component of penguin rehabilitation efforts throughout the region.
author: Euronews

title: Russian General Shot Near Engels Airbase After Ukraine Charges Him Over Hospital Strike
content:
Major General Nikolai Varpakhovich, the commander of a Russian heavy bomber division, was shot twice on Saturday by a gunman on a motorbike near Engels airbase in the Saratov region. The attack occurred as the general was traveling on a military road, and he was subsequently airlifted to a Moscow hospital where he remains in serious condition, according to Russian officials. Ukrainian authorities have previously charged Varpakhovich in absentia for his alleged role in the March 2024 strike on the Okhmatdyt children’s hospital in Kyiv, a claim that Moscow has denied.

The incident adds to a series of targeted attacks on senior Russian military figures amid the ongoing conflict in Ukraine. Russian security services have launched an investigation into the shooting, while Ukrainian officials have not commented on any direct involvement. The health status of Varpakhovich and the outcome of the investigation are expected to influence diplomatic and military calculations in the region.
author: Euronews

title: Iranian café chain manager sentenced to prison and asset seizure for protest-related posts
content:
Sadegh Saeedinia, the manager of the Saeedinia café chain, was sentenced to prison after a court found him guilty of “propaganda against national security.” The conviction stems from Instagram posts in which Saeedinia discussed the January protests and urged his employees to join a strike, actions authorities deemed to undermine state stability.  

Legal analysts note that the ruling represents one of the most severe penalties imposed on a private entrepreneur since the nationwide unrest began, reflecting the government’s broader crackdown on dissent and labor activism linked to the protests. The case underscores the heightened scrutiny of social‑media activity and labor organization in the post‑protest environment.
author: Euronews

title: Russia orders registration of domestic birds, camels and reindeer
content:
A Russian government decree that came into force on Tuesday mandates the registration of certain domestic animals, including birds, camels and reindeer. The regulation, issued by the Ministry of Agriculture, requires owners to submit information about these animals to local authorities, ostensibly to improve veterinary oversight and traceability. The decree lists specific categories of birds—such as chickens, ducks and geese—alongside camels and reindeer, and outlines a filing process that involves submitting documentation to regional registration offices.

Following the announcement, many citizens arrived at government service centres carrying live chickens and other animals, fearing that the law required physical presentation of the livestock for registration. Within hours, officials clarified that owners need only provide the required paperwork and do not have to bring the animals to the offices. The clarification aimed to ease the confusion and streamline compliance, allowing the registration to be completed through standard documentation channels without the need for on‑site animal inspection.
author: Euronews

title: Two suspects arrested after alleged arson attempt at Munich defence firms
content:
Munich police arrested a man and a woman on suspicion of attempting to set fire to the premises of two defence contractors on the city’s industrial outskirts. According to a statement from the Bavarian State Police, the suspects were detained shortly after investigators observed suspicious activity near the facilities and responded to reports of a potential arson threat. Both individuals are being held in custody pending further questioning, and the police have not disclosed their identities or any alleged motives.

The investigation is ongoing, with authorities examining whether the incident was part of a broader security concern targeting the defence sector. Police have indicated that no damage was inflicted on the companies’ property and that no injuries were reported. Officials emphasized that heightened security measures remain in place around critical infrastructure, and they urged the public to report any suspicious behavior that could jeopardize public safety.
author: Euronews

title: Russia conducts reconnaissance in drained Kakhovka Dam area
content:
Russian troops have been advancing in small units across the exposed floor of the Kakhovka reservoir, a region that has remained largely inaccessible since the dam was destroyed in June 2023. The breach flooded the area, creating a vast “no‑man’s land” that has since dried out, exposing the former waterway and allowing limited movement along its banks.

According to a military analyst, the ongoing infiltration is aimed at gathering intelligence rather than preparing a larger offensive. The expert noted that the limited scale of the incursions and their focus on reconnaissance suggest a tactical effort to assess Ukrainian positions and terrain, rather than a sign of an imminent major assault. The activity underscores the evolving dynamics of the conflict in the southern front, where both sides continue to adapt to the altered landscape.
author: France 24

title: French agriculture output falls 8% due to heatwaves
content:
France’s recent heatwaves and accompanying drought have triggered a dual crisis, straining public health and curbing economic activity. Government estimates indicate that the extreme weather has sharply reduced agricultural output, with sector‑generated wealth projected to fall by roughly 8% over the course of the year. The downturn reflects lower crop yields and disrupted supply chains, compounding the broader challenges posed by soaring temperatures that have already heightened health risks across the country.

The agricultural slowdown is expected to ripple through the national economy, trimming France’s growth forecast by an estimated 0.1 percentage point in 2026. Analysts note that the modest yet measurable impact underscores the vulnerability of key sectors to climate‑related events, prompting calls for enhanced resilience measures. Policymakers are monitoring the situation closely as they assess longer‑term strategies to mitigate similar economic setbacks from future heatwaves.
author: France 24

title: US energy firms sign multi-billion-dollar deals with Venezuela
content:
U.S. energy companies signed a series of multi‑billion‑dollar contracts with Venezuela on Wednesday, shortly after the South American nation announced that it would grant American firms control over a substantial portion of its oil reserves. The agreements, which involve several major U.S. operators, were highlighted by President Donald Trump as “the biggest oil deal in world history,” underscoring the administration’s emphasis on expanding American influence in the region’s energy sector. The deals come amid a broader effort by Washington to secure access to Venezuela’s vast hydrocarbon resources despite longstanding U.S. sanctions and a deteriorating Venezuelan economy.

International observers, including France 24 International Affairs Editor Kethevane Gorjestani, have raised concerns that the arrangement could compromise Venezuela’s sovereignty, noting that ceding operational control of its oil fields to foreign entities may limit the government’s ability to direct its own natural‑resource policy. Analysts point to the timing of the contracts, which follow a contentious political climate and ongoing diplomatic negotiations, as a factor that could reshape the balance of power in the country’s oil industry. The outcomes of the deals remain to be seen, but they mark a significant development in U.S.–Venezuelan energy relations and could have lasting implications for regional geopolitics.
author: France 24

title: Two Palestinian teens killed in West Bank raid by Israeli settlers and army
content:
Two Palestinian teenagers were killed on Wednesday during an incident in the village of al‑Mughayyir in the occupied West Bank, according to local officials and the Palestinian Health Ministry. The deaths occurred as Israeli settler militants and Israeli army troops entered the village, an action the Israeli military described as a security operation to protect police officers and an Israeli civilian who was attempting to retrieve livestock. The confrontation took place amid a reported increase in violence by Jewish settlers in the territory, heightening concerns over civilian safety in the area.

The Israeli Defense Forces issued a statement saying their forces moved into al‑Mughayyir to ensure the safety of the police and the civilian involved, while Palestinian authorities have called for an investigation into the killings. The incident adds to a series of recent clashes between settlers and Palestinian residents, underscoring the volatile security situation in the West Bank. Both sides have reiterated their positions, and the event is expected to draw further scrutiny from international observers monitoring the conflict.
author: France 24

title: WMO warns El Nino may become strongest in 40 years
content:
The United Nations’ climate agency warned Thursday that the upcoming El Niño could become the strongest on record since systematic observations began four decades ago, placing the planet in what UN Secretary‑General António Guterres described as a “danger zone of extreme weather.” The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said the naturally occurring climate pattern is expected to intensify to a “very strong” level in the coming months and is “near certain” to persist through February, raising the likelihood of heatwaves, heavy rainfall, droughts and other climate‑related disruptions worldwide.

The forecast underscores heightened concerns among scientists and policymakers about the cumulative impact of a powerful El Niño on already stressed ecosystems and vulnerable communities. As the phenomenon develops, the WMO and UN agencies will monitor its evolution and coordinate with national governments to mitigate adverse effects. France 24 journalist Carys Garland reported on the agency’s statements, highlighting the urgent need for preparedness as the world confronts an extended period of heightened weather volatility.
author: France 24

title: Christian man murdered in Homs, suspect cites personal dispute
content:
A Christian man identified as Nader Boulos Tannous was found dead in Homs, Syria, on 15 August 2026. The killing prompted immediate condemnation from the governments of Israel, Greece and Cyprus, which described the act as an anti‑Christian incident and called for a thorough investigation. Local authorities opened a homicide inquiry and secured the crime scene while diplomatic representatives expressed concern over religiously motivated violence in the region.

Days later, Homs police announced that a suspect had confessed to the murder, stating it stemmed from a personal dispute dating back to 2012 rather than a sectarian motive. Investigators said the confession would be examined alongside forensic evidence as the case proceeds through the Syrian judicial system. The development underscores the complexity of the incident and the authorities’ effort to determine the precise circumstances surrounding Tannous’s death.
author: France 24

title: Nepal worker survives flood‑hit hydropower tunnel, recounts escape
content:
A Nepalese laborer who survived last week’s catastrophic flood recounted a harrowing escape from a tunnel at a hydropower project, saying he fled through a narrow passage as water surged through the underground conduit. The incident is part of a broader disaster that has inundated the country’s mountainous regions, prompting emergency crews to search for workers still inside the tunnels of six hydroelectric plants.

Authorities from Nepal and neighboring China reported that roughly 900 workers remain trapped in the flooded tunnels, while the official death toll from the Himalayan flood rose to 5,624 on Thursday. Rescue teams continue to work around the clock to locate and extract the missing, and officials have warned that the full extent of the damage to the nation’s hydropower infrastructure may take weeks to assess.
author: France 24

title: Norway seizes Russian vessel in Svalbard following Ukrainian court order
content:
Norwegian authorities have detained the Russian-flagged vessel Professor Molchanov following a court order obtained by Ukraine’s state gas company Naftogaz. The order, issued by a Norwegian court, mandates the seizure as collateral for unpaid damages that Naftogaz claims Russia has refused to settle. The ship, which was operating in international waters near Norway’s coast, was taken into custody on the basis of the legal claim presented by Naftogaz.

The Russian government has lodged a formal protest, arguing that the seizure violates international maritime norms and constitutes an unjustified punitive measure. Norwegian officials, however, affirmed that the action complies with domestic law and the court’s ruling, emphasizing that the detention is a civil enforcement step rather than a political sanction. The case underscores ongoing tensions between Russia and Ukraine over energy‑related disputes and may set a precedent for similar asset seizures linked to cross‑border commercial claims.
author: DW World

title: UN report says foreign recruitment and external support fuel Sudan war
content:
Foreign recruitment and external support networks are intensifying the conflict in Sudan, according to a new report released Thursday by independent United Nations human‑rights investigators. The investigators said that the influx of foreign fighters and the provision of weapons, training and financial resources from abroad are sustaining the fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which has persisted since the power struggle erupted in April 2023.

The report calls for urgent accountability measures, urging the international community to investigate and sanction entities that facilitate the recruitment and supply chains that empower both sides. It also stresses the need for stronger monitoring of cross‑border movements and financial flows to curb the external drivers of the war, as civilian casualties and displacement continue to rise amid the ongoing clashes.
author: UN News

title: UN Security Council meets on Syria's chemical weapons and undisclosed nuclear material
content:
The United Nations nuclear watchdog disclosed that the former Syrian regime did not report the possession of nuclear material, adding to earlier concerns after an undeclared chemical‑weapons cache was uncovered in May. The International Atomic Energy Agency’s findings indicate that the material was not included in Syria’s declared inventory, raising questions about the completeness of the country’s compliance with its non‑proliferation obligations. The chemical‑weapons discovery, which involved a stockpile hidden from international inspectors, further underscores gaps in the verification regime governing Syria’s weapons programs.

In response, the United Nations Security Council convened on Thursday to receive a briefing on the new information and to consider possible next steps. Delegates examined the implications for regional security and discussed options for enhancing monitoring and enforcement mechanisms. The council’s deliberations are expected to shape future actions aimed at ensuring full transparency and compliance with international arms‑control agreements in Syria.
author: UN News

title: Gloria Steinem, Prominent Feminist Journalist, Dies at 92
content:
Gloria Steinem, the journalist and women's‑rights activist who emerged as a leading voice of the feminist movement, died on Wednesday at the age of 92. Her family announced the passing on Instagram, noting that she died at her New York City home surrounded by loved ones.

Steinem’s career spanned six decades and included co‑founding *Ms.* magazine, organizing national women’s marches, and serving as a prominent advocate for gender equality in the United States and abroad. Her work helped shape public discourse on reproductive rights, workplace discrimination, and political representation, cementing her legacy as one of the most influential figures in modern feminism.
author: UN News

title: Machado says Venezuela's interim government lacks authority to sign US oil deal
content:
Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado publicly questioned the legitimacy of the United States‑Venezuela oil agreement announced by President Donald Trump last Friday, describing the interim government in Caracas as lacking a democratic mandate to negotiate the country’s natural resources. Machado asserted that the nation’s oil and gas reserves do not belong to “an illegitimate regime,” and warned that any deal struck with the interim authorities could undermine Venezuela’s sovereignty.

The agreement, which Trump hailed as “the biggest oil deal in world history,” was presented as a breakthrough in U.S. policy toward the oil‑rich nation after months of diplomatic isolation. Machado’s remarks marked her first public comments since the deal’s announcement, and she emphasized the need for a government elected through free and fair elections before any resource negotiations can be considered valid. While criticizing the pact, she also sought to avoid a direct confrontation with the White House, walking a diplomatic tightrope between opposition to the deal and maintaining channels for future dialogue.

Analysts note that Machado’s statements could complicate the nascent relationship between Washington and the Venezuelan interim administration, which has been seeking international recognition while contending with internal political challenges. The opposition’s stance may pressure the United States to reassess the terms of the oil arrangement or to seek broader consensus within Venezuela before proceeding with further energy cooperation.
author: Guardian World

title: Houthi fighters clash with Yemeni government forces in southwest, targeting Taiz‑al‑Makha road
content:
The Houthi movement has launched an operation to block the main highway that connects the city of Taiz with the coastal town of al‑Makha, a route that the internationally recognized Yemeni government relies on to transport food, fuel and military supplies to its southern strongholds. According to statements from Yemeni government officials, the rebels placed explosive devices and erected barricades along the road on Monday, forcing convoy traffic to be rerouted through longer, less secure desert tracks. The maneuver comes amid intensified fighting in the Taiz governorate, where government forces have been attempting to regain control of the city after months of stalemate, and follows a series of Houthi attacks on supply lines across the country.

Analysts note that severing the Taiz‑al‑Makha corridor could hamper the government's logistical capacity in the south and increase pressure on the coalition‑backed forces operating in the region. The road is also a key conduit for humanitarian aid destined for millions of civilians displaced by the conflict. While the Houthis have not issued a formal declaration of intent, the move is viewed as part of a broader strategy to undermine the government's operational reach. Both sides have called for an immediate cessation of hostilities, but the disruption of the supply route underscores the ongoing volatility of Yemen’s war and its impact on the delivery of essential services.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Raul Asencio acquitted of sex‑tape sharing charges, faces club discipline over drink‑driving conviction
content:
Real Madrid have launched formal disciplinary proceedings against midfielder Álvaro Asencio after he was convicted of drink‑driving earlier this month. The club’s statement, released on Tuesday, said the investigation will assess whether the conviction breaches the organization’s internal code of conduct and could result in sanctions ranging from fines to suspension.

Asencio, who joined the first‑team squad in 2022, was found guilty of operating a vehicle with a blood‑alcohol level above the legal limit and received a three‑month driving ban and a €600 fine from the court. While the legal case is separate from his football duties, the club emphasized its commitment to upholding professional standards and will announce any disciplinary measures after the review is completed.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Gaza dentists provide care on streets amid Israeli siege
content:
Gaza’s ongoing humanitarian crisis has left dental care largely inaccessible, with limited supplies and a shortage of functional clinics turning routine procedures into a luxury for most residents. The United Nations Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA) reports that only a handful of dental units remain operational in the enclave, many of which lack essential equipment, sterilization materials, and basic consumables such as fillings and anesthetics.

The scarcity of office space for dental practices further compounds the problem, as many former clinics have been repurposed for emergency medical services or destroyed in recent conflicts. Consequently, patients with urgent dental needs often endure prolonged pain or resort to informal, unregulated treatment options, while routine check‑ups and preventive care are largely unavailable. Health officials warn that the continued lack of dental services could exacerbate broader public health concerns, prompting calls for increased humanitarian assistance to restore essential oral health infrastructure in Gaza.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Israeli airstrike captured behind journalist in Lebanese village
content:
A journalist reporting from a village in southern Lebanon captured a striking image of an Israeli airstrike unfolding behind them on Monday, as the correspondent described the ongoing hostilities along the Israel‑Lebanon border. The footage, aired by an international news agency, showed a plume of smoke rising from a residential area while the reporter continued the on‑the‑ground interview, highlighting the immediacy of the conflict for civilians in the region. The village, located a few kilometres north of the disputed Shebaa Farms, has been a frequent flashpoint since the escalation that began in early October, when cross‑border exchanges between Israeli forces and Hezbollah intensified.

The incident comes amid a broader pattern of retaliatory strikes following a series of rocket launches from southern Lebanon into northern Israel and subsequent Israeli air operations targeting what it described as Hezbollah positions and weapons caches. Israeli officials declined to comment on the specific strike captured in the broadcast, while Lebanese authorities condemned the attack as a violation of sovereignty and called for international attention to the civilian impact. The visual evidence of the bombing underscores the heightened volatility of the border area and the challenges faced by journalists covering the conflict in real time.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Legal battle over mail-in voting regulations intensifies ahead of November midterms
content:
As the United States prepares for the November midterm elections, a growing legal dispute is unfolding over new attempts to tighten regulations on mail‑in voting. Several states have introduced or enacted measures that would restrict the use of absentee ballots, impose stricter verification requirements, or limit the number of drop‑off locations, prompting civil‑rights groups, election officials, and political parties to file lawsuits challenging the constitutionality and practicality of the changes. Federal and state courts have already heard arguments that the proposed rules could disenfranchise voters, particularly seniors, people with disabilities, and those living in rural areas who rely on postal ballots.

The litigation, which spans multiple jurisdictions, includes challenges filed in federal district courts and state supreme courts, with plaintiffs seeking injunctions to halt enforcement of the new rules before the election. Defendants, typically state election boards or governors, argue that the regulations are necessary to safeguard election integrity and prevent fraud. Judges have so far issued a mix of temporary stays and denials, leaving the ultimate fate of the mail‑in voting restrictions uncertain as the election calendar tightens. The outcome of these cases will determine whether the upcoming midterms will proceed under the newly proposed constraints or maintain the broader mail‑in voting procedures that have been in place since the pandemic.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Canada prepared for mutually beneficial US trade deal, says Carney
content:
Mark Carney, the former governor of the Bank of Canada and current chair of the Bank for International Settlements, said Canada is prepared to finalize a trade arrangement that delivers mutual benefits for businesses and workers on both sides of the border. Speaking at a bilateral economic forum in Ottawa, Carry emphasized that the Canadian government is seeking a deal that safeguards employment, supports competitive industries, and enhances cross‑border investment while addressing the concerns raised by stakeholders in both countries.

Carney’s remarks come as the United States and Canada continue to refine the terms of the United States‑Mexico‑Canada Agreement (USMCA) and explore additional bilateral initiatives aimed at modernising trade in sectors such as automotive manufacturing, agriculture, technology, and clean energy. Canadian officials have highlighted the importance of maintaining labour standards, protecting supply‑chain resilience, and ensuring that any new provisions do not disadvantage domestic workers. The United States has indicated a willingness to engage in discussions that align with its own economic priorities, setting the stage for negotiations that could culminate in a comprehensive agreement before the end of the fiscal year. If successful, the deal would reinforce the long‑standing economic partnership between the two nations and provide a framework for future cooperation.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Trump calls media treasonous over reports of Iran war munitions shortage
content:
The president on Tuesday launched a fresh criticism of news outlets that have highlighted what experts describe as “troubling shortages” of essential goods across the country. In a televised address, the head of state accused several media organizations of sensationalizing supply‑chain disruptions and undermining public confidence in the government’s response. He asserted that the reports were “overblown” and urged journalists to focus on the steps being taken to stabilize the market, including recent policy measures aimed at boosting domestic production and expediting imports.

Analysts and consumer‑rights groups, however, say the shortages—particularly of medical supplies, fuel and staple foods—remain significant and are exacerbated by logistical bottlenecks and rising demand. Independent data from the national statistics office shows a 12 percent decline in pharmacy inventories of certain medications over the past month, while fuel stations in several regions reported intermittent out‑of‑stock periods. The president’s remarks have drawn mixed reactions: media watchdogs defended their coverage as “necessary oversight,” while the administration pledged to increase transparency and accelerate relief efforts to address the gaps identified by experts.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Anthony Joshua's driver charged with causing death by dangerous driving in Nigeria
content:
Adeniyi Mobolaji Kayode has been formally charged in Nigeria with a series of offences, the most serious of which is causing death by dangerous driving. The charges were filed by the Federal Capital Territory Police Command following an investigation into a road‑traffic incident that resulted in a fatality. Kayode, identified as the driver of the vehicle involved, is now facing criminal prosecution under the country's Road Traffic Act.

The indictment includes additional counts related to reckless conduct and failure to render assistance at the scene, reflecting the authorities’ assessment that the driver’s actions directly contributed to the loss of life. If convicted, Kayode could be subject to imprisonment, fines, and a possible revocation of his driving licence, in line with Nigerian sentencing guidelines for dangerous driving offences. The case is scheduled for a preliminary hearing next month, after which the court will determine whether it proceeds to trial.
author: BBC World

title: Rocket Lab Delays First Private Venus Mission Due to Neutron Readiness
content:
The first privately‑funded mission to Venus has been postponed, with the spacecraft remaining on the ground while Rocket Lab’s Neutron launch vehicle encounters technical setbacks. The delay comes as the team prepares for a launch that was originally targeted for late 2024, but a series of engineering reviews and component testing have pushed the schedule back.

Despite the setback, mission officials have expressed confidence that the project will still achieve its objectives. The spacecraft, designed to study Venus’s atmosphere and surface conditions, will benefit from the additional time to refine its systems and conduct thorough pre‑flight testing. Rocket Lab’s Neutron, a reusable heavy‑lift rocket, is expected to be ready for a future launch window once the remaining issues are resolved.

The team’s optimism underscores the significance of the mission as a milestone for commercial space exploration. Once the launch vehicle is cleared, the private venture will represent a new chapter in planetary science, demonstrating the growing role of private companies in deep‑space missions.
author: Space.com

title: India to launch first geosynchronous Earth-imaging satellite on Sept. 3
content:
India’s space agency, the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), is set to attempt a historic launch on September 3, targeting a geosynchronous orbit for an Earth‑imaging satellite—a trajectory the nation has not yet achieved successfully. The mission, scheduled to lift off from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre using the PSLV‑C55 launch vehicle, will place the satellite at approximately 35,800 km above the equator, allowing it to remain fixed over a single point on Earth and provide continuous high‑resolution imagery.

If successful, the launch would mark India’s first operational geostationary Earth observation platform, expanding its capabilities for weather monitoring, disaster management and commercial imaging services. ISRO officials have made a live webcast of the countdown and launch available to the public, inviting viewers worldwide to witness the event as it unfolds. The outcome will be closely watched by both domestic and international observers as a benchmark of India’s growing proficiency in advanced orbital deployments.
author: Space.com

title: 606 miles in six days: teacher Megan Eckert chases ultrarunning history – and a men’s record
content:
Middle‑school math teacher Megan Eckert of Santa Fe, New Mexico, will leave her classroom for the Global Organization of Multi‑Day Ultramarathoners (GOMU) World Championship this week, joining more than 100 athletes at the start line in Balatonfüred, Hungary. The six‑day event, slated to begin Thursday, challenges participants to cover the greatest possible distance within 144 hours, a format that has produced record‑breaking performances in recent years. Eckert, the current women’s world‑record holder for the 144‑hour distance, once described a 5 kilometre run as daunting, yet she now aims to extend her own mark and surpass the United States men’s record for the same duration.

Organizers expect a fiercely competitive field as runners push the limits of endurance, with the ultimate goal of setting new benchmarks in ultra‑distance running. Eckert’s participation underscores the growing prominence of multi‑day ultramarathons on the global stage, and her attempt to eclipse both her personal best and the national men’s record will be closely watched by the ultrarunning community. The championship concludes after six days, at which point the final distances will determine the new world and national record holders.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Benhard Janse van Rensburg denies Erasmus claim of Springboks call‑up talks
content:
Centre Benhard Janse van Rensburg responded to recent rumours that he had been in talks with the South African Rugby Union about a Springboks call‑up. In a statement released to the press, the 27‑year‑old centre, who currently plies his trade with the French Top 14 club Stade Rugby Bordeaux, said he “probably would have loved to” play for his native South Africa. He added that the claims made by former Springboks head coach Rassie Erasmus were unfounded and that no formal discussions had taken place.

Janse van Rensburg, who earned his first cap for the Springboks in 2021, has been a regular starter for Bordeaux since 2022. The player’s spokesperson clarified that while the South African national team has expressed interest in his services, no concrete offers or negotiations have been made. The former Springboks coach, who stepped down after the 2023 Rugby World Cup, reportedly suggested that the centre was being considered for future squads, a statement that the player denies.

The centre’s comments come amid a broader debate over the selection of overseas‑based players for the Springboks. Janse van Rensburg has indicated that his focus remains on his club commitments in France and that any future international involvement would depend on formal invitations from the South African Rugby Union.
author: BBC Sport

title: I used to play in-match games as a laugh - Dean
content:
Former Premier League referee Mike Dean, who officiated more than 400 top‑flight matches over a 25‑year career, disclosed in a recent interview that he deliberately remained in the centre circle for as long as possible during games. Dean explained that staying close to the kickoff spot gave him a clearer view of the opening phases of play, allowing him to assess player positioning and potential fouls before the ball moved into the wider areas of the pitch. He added that the proximity helped him maintain optimal communication with his assistants and the fourth official, ensuring that any early incidents could be addressed promptly.

Dean’s comment reflects a broader emphasis on positioning that he has highlighted throughout his tenure, noting that early‑match vigilance can set the tone for the remainder of the contest. The former official retired from active refereeing in 2022 and has since contributed to referee development programs, where he continues to stress the importance of initial positioning for aspiring officials. His remarks provide insight into the practical considerations that underpin elite match officiating.
author: BBC Sport

title: Former Air Force Secretary Kendall Calls Hegseth’s Pentagon Dysfunctional
content:
Former Secretary of the Air Force Frank Kendall III denounced the Defense Department under Secretary Pete Hegseth as “dysfunctional” during a Wednesday interview with CNN’s Kaitlan Collins.  Kendall, who served as Secretary of the Air Force from 2017 to 2021 and previously held a senior acquisition post under President Barack Obama, said Hegseth’s leadership has “done active damage” to the Pentagon’s ability to manage its workforce and budget.  He cited a pattern of misaligned priorities, a lack of clear direction for the military, and an environment in which senior leaders feel “over‑controlled” and “under‑informed.”

Kendall’s remarks come amid growing scrutiny of Hegseth’s performance, including questions over the department’s handling of procurement delays, cybersecurity incidents, and morale at the base level.  The former secretary urged the department to adopt a more collaborative approach, noting that the current climate “creates a culture of fear and uncertainty.”  Hegseth has defended his record, emphasizing recent reforms aimed at streamlining acquisition processes and improving accountability.

The comments add to a chorus of criticism from former military officials who argue that Hegseth’s tenure has weakened the Pentagon’s operational readiness.  Whether the Department of Defense will respond with policy changes remains to be seen, but Kendall’s public critique underscores the urgency of addressing the department’s internal challenges.
author: The Hill

title: Sen. Chuck Grassley Posts TikTok Tribute to Family Vacuum Beth
content:
Sen. Chuck Grassley (R‑Iowa) made his first foray onto TikTok on Wednesday, sharing a short video that pays tribute to a long‑time family heirloom—a vacuum cleaner he affectionately calls “Beth.” In the clip, the veteran senator displays a series of photographs chronicling the appliance’s history, from its early days in the family garage to its current state. “Only feels appropriate to pay homage to Beth,” he wrote in the caption, underscoring the sentimental value the device holds for him and his relatives.

The video, which quickly attracted a modest following on the platform, illustrates Grassley’s willingness to engage with younger audiences through a popular social‑media channel. By spotlighting a mundane household item, the senator offers a light‑hearted glimpse into his personal life, a contrast to his long tenure in the Senate and his reputation for focusing on fiscal and agricultural issues. The post demonstrates how even seasoned politicians are exploring new digital avenues to connect with constituents.

Grassley’s TikTok debut signals a broader trend of public officials using short‑form video to humanize themselves and reach a wider demographic. While the post itself is brief, it highlights the senator’s adaptability and willingness to embrace contemporary communication tools, potentially broadening his appeal among younger voters.
author: The Hill

title: Genocide Accusations Must Be Applied Equally, Not Targeted
content:
A United Nations panel has formally accused Nation X of violating international humanitarian law for its conduct in the eastern province of its territory. The accusation, unprecedented in its severity, cites the systematic targeting of civilian infrastructure and the use of prohibited weaponry—acts that, according to the panel, constitute war crimes under the Geneva Convention. The panel’s report notes that similar conduct by other states in comparable conflict zones has not yet triggered comparable investigations or sanctions.

Nation X’s foreign ministry immediately rejected the allegations, labeling them “unsubstantiated and politically motivated.” The report, however, cites multiple independent satellite images, intercepted communications, and testimonies from displaced residents, all of which corroborate the panel’s findings. While the panel’s findings are being debated in international legal circles, observers point out that no other country has faced a similar level of scrutiny for comparable violations in the past decade, raising concerns about selective enforcement and potential geopolitical bias.

The international community remains divided. Human rights organizations have called for an independent inquiry and for the enforcement of the panel’s recommendations, while several allied nations have urged restraint, citing the need for diplomatic engagement. As the debate continues, the focus shifts to whether the panel’s actions represent a genuine pursuit of justice or a strategic move aimed at advancing broader geopolitical objectives.
author: The Hill

title: NASA Chief Isaacman Outlines First Steps for Moon Base
content:
NASA’s plans for a permanent lunar outpost have been highlighted by flight‑director Ethan Isaacman, who said the base will “help NASA learn how to live away from Earth, and possibly later to Mars and other planets.”  The proposed habitat, part of the Artemis program, is slated to be established on the Moon’s near side by the late 2020s.  Isaacman noted that the site will serve as a testing ground for life‑support systems, habitat construction, and surface operations that are essential for any future deep‑space missions.

The lunar base will be equipped with modular living quarters, research laboratories, and a robotic maintenance team, allowing astronauts to conduct experiments in a low‑gravity environment while also evaluating the feasibility of long‑duration stays.  By studying how humans adapt to the Moon’s harsh conditions—extreme temperatures, radiation, and limited resources—NASA aims to refine the technologies and protocols needed for sustained exploration on Mars and beyond.  The initiative also aligns with international partners, who plan to contribute scientific instruments and support infrastructure.

If successful, the Moon base could become a critical stepping stone for humanity’s next frontier.  Isaacman emphasized that the knowledge gained will reduce risks and costs for future missions to Mars, making the dream of interplanetary travel increasingly attainable.  The project’s progress will be closely monitored as it moves from concept to construction, marking a pivotal moment in space exploration history.
author: The Hill

title: Bacon backs Tillis on Hegseth removal
content:
Rep. Don Bacon (R‑Neb.) confirmed on a Wednesday interview that he shares the concerns voiced by Senator Thom Tillis (R‑N.C.) about the current leadership of the Department of Defense. Bacon, who serves on the House Armed Services Committee, said he agrees with Tillis’s sentiment that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s performance has raised questions among lawmakers. “I hate to tell the president who he should hire and fire,” Bacon remarked, noting that the decision ultimately lies with the administration.

The remarks come amid growing criticism of Hegseth’s handling of several defense matters, including procurement delays and oversight of the Army’s modernization program. Both Bacon and Tillis have called for a review of Hegseth’s record, suggesting that a change in leadership could better align the department with congressional expectations. While Bacon declined to specify the criteria for a replacement, he emphasized the need for accountability and effective management within the defense establishment.

In summary, Rep. Bacon’s statement reinforces bipartisan pressure on President Biden to consider a new Defense Secretary. The conversation underscores ongoing concerns about Hegseth’s stewardship and reflects a broader congressional push for leadership that can address the department’s operational and strategic challenges.
author: The Hill

title: September Brings Shorter Days: Daylight Decline Explained
content:
Scientists have confirmed that while the Earth’s rotation continues to produce a 24‑hour day, the total amount of daylight received each day is gradually decreasing. Long‑term astronomical observations and satellite data show a measurable, though small, decline in daylight hours at mid‑latitude and higher latitudes over the past few centuries. The effect is most noticeable during the transition from summer to winter, when the length of daylight shortens more rapidly than in previous decades.

The decline is driven by the planet’s axial tilt and orbital dynamics. Earth’s axis is slowly wobbling and its tilt is gradually decreasing, a process known as axial precession. As a result, the angle at which the sun’s rays strike the planet changes, shortening the period of daylight during the winter months and lengthening it in the summer. This subtle shift has implications for ecosystems that rely on precise photoperiods, for agricultural calendars, and for human activities that are timed to daylight availability.

Researchers continue to monitor these changes to improve climate and ecological models. While the 24‑hour day remains constant, the gradual reduction in daylight underscores the need for adaptive strategies in agriculture, energy management, and wildlife conservation. Understanding the underlying astronomical mechanisms helps scientists predict future photoperiod shifts and their potential impacts on both natural and human systems.
author: The Hill

title: 77 Black Women Secure Congressional Ballot Spots Ahead of November Elections
content:
Nearly all of this year’s primary contests have wrapped up, leaving 77 Black women on the ballot for the upcoming midterm elections. The candidates span a range of offices, from local city councils to statewide seats, and include a mix of incumbents seeking reelection and newcomers challenging open positions. Their presence marks a significant increase in Black female representation compared to previous election cycles.

The surge reflects broader efforts to diversify political participation, supported by targeted outreach and fundraising initiatives from national and grassroots organizations. Analysts note that the candidates’ platforms cover issues such as criminal justice reform, affordable housing, and economic equity, aligning with the priorities of many voters in historically underrepresented communities. Early polling data suggests that these candidates could influence outcomes in several key districts, potentially reshaping the partisan balance in state legislatures.

As the midterms approach, campaign teams are intensifying voter engagement efforts, while election officials prepare to accommodate the expanded slate of candidates. The presence of 77 Black women on the ballot underscores a growing trend toward greater inclusivity in American politics and highlights the importance of representation in shaping legislative agendas.
author: The Hill

title: Hillary Clinton mourns Gloria Steinem's death
content:
Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton expressed deep sorrow over the passing of feminist icon Gloria Steinem, describing herself as “heartsick.”  Steinem, who died at her New York City home on Wednesday at the age of 92, was widely recognized as an architect of women’s equality and a leading activist in the feminist movement.

Clinton’s statement, “Oh, Gayle, I’m heartsick, as I think everyone who not only knew her but followed…,” was shared on Thursday, underscoring the broad impact Steinem had on both political and social spheres.  Her career spanned decades of advocacy, journalism, and public service, earning her a place among the most influential figures in the fight for gender equality.

The loss of Steinem marks a significant moment for the feminist community and the broader public.  Her legacy continues to inspire activists, policymakers, and ordinary citizens committed to advancing women’s rights worldwide.
author: The Hill

title: Burnham commits to 3.5% defence spending by 2035, not 3% by 2030
content:
Andy Burnham, the newly appointed UK defence secretary, has announced that the United Kingdom will aim to meet NATO’s 3.5 % defence‑spending target by 2035. In a statement released this week, Burnham clarified that the country will not be able to reach the 3 % threshold by the 2030 deadline that many NATO members have set for themselves.

The decision reflects a recalibration of the UK’s defence budget in light of current fiscal constraints and strategic priorities. Burnham noted that while the 3 % target remains a long‑term goal, achieving it by 2035 allows the government to balance investment in modernising forces with other public spending commitments. The move also signals a continued commitment to NATO’s collective defence framework, even as the UK adjusts its timeline to align with realistic economic conditions.

Burnham’s announcement was met with a mixture of support and caution from defence analysts, who point out that the extended timeline may affect the pace of procurement and readiness initiatives. Nonetheless, the pledge underscores the UK’s ongoing effort to strengthen its military capabilities while navigating the broader economic landscape.
author: BBC Politics

title: Experts urge more support for renewable energy in Africa's food systems
content:
Renewable energy is increasingly seen as a catalyst for higher productivity and greater competitiveness among African food businesses, yet a range of barriers limits its uptake. Experts who spoke to *Climate Home News* argue that while solar and wind power could reduce operating costs and improve supply‑chain reliability, the high initial investment required, fragmented local markets, and a scarcity of tailored financing options remain significant hurdles.

The challenges are compounded by a lack of coordinated policy frameworks and limited access to low‑interest loans or subsidies for small‑to‑medium enterprises. Without targeted support from governments, development banks, and private investors, many food producers will struggle to transition to clean energy, leaving them vulnerable to volatile fuel prices and supply disruptions. The experts call for a concerted effort to create financing mechanisms, streamline market entry, and build technical capacity to unlock the full potential of renewables across Africa’s food sector.
author: Climate Home News

title: NYC Plastic Waste Overwhelms City, Residents Respond
content:
Photographer Bryan Anselm has spent several months documenting the pervasive presence of plastic waste in urban and rural settings, from the congested streets of New York City to the quieter neighborhoods of Quebec. His images reveal how discarded plastic—wrappers, bags, and bottles—overflows bins, clogs gutters, and becomes a visible layer of the cityscape, a phenomenon he captures in stark, high‑contrast shots that emphasize the material’s persistence.

Anselm’s work highlights both the scale of the problem and the grassroots responses underway to mitigate it. In New York, the lack of hidden alleys means that recycling bags and other refuse are often left in plain sight, making the waste a public spectacle. In Quebec, community groups have organized clean‑up drives and educational campaigns to reduce single‑use plastics. The photographer’s images echo literary observations, such as Nick Shay’s claim in Don DeLillo’s *Underworld* that “garbage is not what we cast out, but the prime locus of meaning in our lives,” underscoring how waste shapes cultural and environmental narratives.

The series serves as a visual record of the ongoing struggle against plastic pollution and a call to action for both policymakers and citizens. By documenting the everyday realities of waste accumulation and the efforts to counter it, Anselm’s work invites viewers to confront the environmental footprint of modern consumption and to consider the collective responsibility for a cleaner, more sustainable future.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Limiting Junk Food Ads on Public Transport Could Reduce Obesity Costs
content:
Fast‑food advertising on public transport has been linked to higher consumption of unhealthy foods and drinks, a trend that is driving obesity rates across Australia.  Studies show that eye‑catching ads placed on buses and at train stations encourage impulse purchases, especially among young adults and families who are already exposed to a high volume of marketing messages.

The health‑care and social costs of this obesity epidemic are staggering.  According to recent estimates, the Australian government and society spend roughly A$39 billion each year on obesity‑related health care, lost productivity, and associated chronic diseases.  The figure highlights the economic burden of diet‑related health problems and the potential savings that could be achieved through stricter advertising regulations or public‑health campaigns.

Policymakers and health advocates are calling for tighter controls on fast‑food marketing in public spaces.  If the government were to limit or ban such advertising, experts suggest that it could reduce the frequency of unhealthy food purchases, lower obesity prevalence, and ultimately cut the annual A$39 billion cost to the nation’s health system.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Metformin May Slow Aging by Activating AMPK
content:
Metformin, the most commonly prescribed medication for type 2 diabetes, is known for its safety, low cost and effectiveness in lowering blood sugar and improving insulin sensitivity. The drug works by mimicking a cellular energy deficit, similar to the state of fasting, which activates the AMP‑activated protein kinase (AMPK) pathway. AMPK promotes cellular waste clearance and repair mechanisms, thereby helping to maintain metabolic health.

A recent review of preclinical and clinical studies has highlighted the possibility that metformin’s activation of AMPK could also mitigate certain biological processes associated with aging. By enhancing cellular cleanup and repair, the drug may slow age‑related decline in tissue function, suggesting a potential role beyond glucose control. The authors note that while the data are promising, further research is needed to confirm these anti‑aging effects in humans.

If future trials confirm metformin’s benefits for aging, the drug could become a low‑cost intervention for age‑related health maintenance. For now, its established use in diabetes management remains the primary indication, with anti‑aging applications still under investigation.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Peptide Supplements: Marketing Outpaces FDA-Approved Uses
content:
Peptides—short chains of amino acids that serve specialized roles in the body—have become a focal point of modern therapeutic research. Among the most recognized examples are insulin and glucagon‑like peptide‑1 (GLP‑1), both of which have received United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval for treating diabetes and related metabolic disorders. These approvals underscore the clinical relevance of peptide‑based drugs and highlight the growing confidence in their safety and efficacy.

Insulin, the hormone that regulates blood glucose, was the first peptide drug to receive FDA approval and remains a cornerstone of type 1 and type 2 diabetes management. GLP‑1 analogues, which mimic the incretin hormone GLP‑1, enhance insulin secretion, suppress glucagon release, and promote satiety, offering a multifaceted approach to glycemic control. The success of these agents has spurred investment in a broader pipeline of peptide therapeutics, including those targeting obesity, cardiovascular disease, and chronic pain.

The continued expansion of FDA‑approved peptide drugs signals a maturation of the field and a promising future for precision medicine. As regulatory pathways become more streamlined and manufacturing techniques improve, peptides are poised to play an increasingly prominent role in treating a wide array of conditions.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Missouri WIC Families Seek More Support
content:
The U.S. Department of Agriculture reports that the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants and Children (WIC) reached an unprecedented 41 % of all U.S. infants during fiscal year 2025. The data, released in the agency’s latest enrollment statistics, indicate that nearly half of the country’s newborns received nutrition assistance through the federal program, which provides healthy food, nutrition education, and breastfeeding support to low‑income families.

WIC’s expanded reach reflects both increased eligibility and broader outreach efforts. The program, which has served millions of children and pregnant or postpartum women since the 1970s, is designed to prevent malnutrition and support healthy growth. In 2025, the 41 % participation rate marked the highest share in the program’s history, underscoring its growing importance in addressing food insecurity among the nation’s most vulnerable populations.

The Department of Agriculture’s findings highlight WIC’s continued role as a critical safety net for families with limited resources. By extending nutrition assistance to a larger portion of infants, the program helps promote early childhood development and reduces long‑term health disparities. The agency plans to maintain and potentially expand its services in the coming years to sustain this level of coverage.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Cannabis Edibles Impair Driving Even Below Legal THC Limits
content:
The psychoactive effects commonly described as a “high” after cannabis consumption are primarily attributed to delta‑9‑tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the principal intoxicating compound in the plant. THC interacts with cannabinoid receptors in the brain, altering perception, mood, and cognition, and is present in a wide range of products, including traditional smoked flower as well as edible forms such as gummies, brownies, and chocolates. Alongside THC, cannabidiol (CBD) is frequently incorporated into cannabis products; unlike THC, CBD does not produce intoxication and is marketed for its potential therapeutic properties, including anxiety relief and anti‑inflammatory effects.

Regulatory agencies and health officials continue to monitor the prevalence of THC‑infused edibles, noting that their delayed onset of action can lead to accidental overconsumption. Public health advisories emphasize the importance of clear labeling, dosage guidance, and consumer education to mitigate risks associated with unintended high levels of THC exposure. Ongoing research aims to clarify the distinct pharmacological profiles of THC and CBD, informing policy decisions and medical guidelines as cannabis products become increasingly accessible.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Zimbabwe sees 12-year increase in average age of tuberculosis diagnosis
content:
More people die from tuberculosis (TB) than from any other infectious disease worldwide, with an estimated 1.2 million deaths recorded in 2025, according to the latest health data. The disease continues to pose a major public‑health challenge, especially in low‑ and middle‑income regions where diagnostic, treatment, and prevention resources remain limited.

In Africa, the continent accounts for roughly one‑quarter of global TB cases, translating into about 315 000 deaths in 2024. The high mortality rate reflects persistent gaps in early detection and access to effective therapy, underscoring the need for intensified control measures and sustained international support to curb the epidemic.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Five subtypes of common liver disease discovered—including rapidly progressing genetic forms
content:
A recent study by Mayo Clinic researchers has revealed that a liver condition affecting nearly 30 % of adults worldwide is not a single disease but actually comprises five biologically distinct subtypes. The investigation, which analyzed large patient cohorts and molecular data, identified these subtypes as having markedly different clinical trajectories and risk profiles.

Each subtype was found to carry its own set of complications. Some patients face a higher likelihood of progressing to heart disease, while others are more prone to liver failure or developing liver cancer. Moreover, the need for liver transplantation varies across the groups, underscoring the importance of precise diagnosis. The study’s authors emphasize that treating the condition as a homogeneous entity may overlook these critical differences, potentially leading to suboptimal management.

The findings suggest that a more nuanced classification could inform personalized treatment strategies and improve prognostication. By tailoring interventions to the specific subtype, clinicians may better mitigate the risk of severe outcomes and enhance patient care.
author: Medical Xpress

title: How severe illness during pregnancy sometimes alters neurodevelopment
content:
Neurodevelopmental conditions—including autism spectrum disorder, attention‑deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and related disorders—affect roughly 10 % of Americans, according to recent epidemiological studies. The high prevalence underscores the importance of understanding these disorders, yet pinpointing their precise onset, etiology, and demographic distribution remains a persistent challenge for researchers and clinicians alike.

Scientists attribute the difficulty to a combination of factors. First, the clinical presentation of neurodevelopmental disorders varies widely among individuals, making early identification inconsistent. Second, diagnostic criteria have evolved over time, and many children receive a diagnosis only after school‑age assessments, which obscures the true age of onset. Third, environmental influences—such as prenatal exposures, early childhood nutrition, and socioeconomic status—interact with genetic predispositions in complex ways that are not yet fully mapped. Consequently, large‑scale longitudinal studies are being designed to track children from birth through adolescence, aiming to clarify the timing and mechanisms that trigger these conditions.

Despite these obstacles, advances in neuroimaging, genomics, and data‑analytic methods are gradually refining our understanding of neurodevelopmental disorders. Continued investment in population‑based research and early screening programs is expected to improve diagnostic accuracy and inform targeted interventions, ultimately reducing the long‑term burden on individuals, families, and healthcare systems.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Dutch Central Bank Transfers 86 Tonnes of Gold to London Amid Geopolitical Unrest
content:
De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB) announced that it has transferred 86 tonnes of its gold reserves from the United States and Canada to London, citing “increasing geopolitical unrest” as the primary reason for the move. The Dutch central bank said that gold held in London can be traded more readily than the holdings in New York and Ottawa, giving it greater flexibility to respond swiftly if a crisis were to arise.

The relocation reflects a broader trend among central banks to diversify storage locations and reduce exposure to any single country’s political or economic risks. By concentrating a significant portion of its gold in the United Kingdom, DNB aims to streamline access to its reserves and potentially lower transaction costs in times of market volatility. The decision follows the bank’s assessment that London’s gold market infrastructure offers more efficient liquidity and tighter settlement timelines than the North American facilities.

DNB’s move underscores the growing importance of strategic reserve management in an uncertain global environment. While the bank did not disclose any immediate operational changes, it emphasized that the new arrangement will enable a quicker and more effective response to any sudden market disruptions, thereby strengthening the resilience of the Dutch monetary system.
author: Guardian Business

title: European Bond Yields Dip as Market Turmoil Eases
content: European government borrowing costs are declining this morning, with yields on benchmark 10-year bonds falling across major economies. The yield on 10-year German bunds has decreased by 1.5 basis points to 3.36%, while French 10-year bond
author: Guardian Business

title: North Sea Workers Must Weigh Under 19.5 Stone for New Helicopter Safety Rules
content:
A new safety guideline has been issued for workers operating in environments where winching to a rescue point is required. The regulation stipulates that personnel must not weigh more than 19.5 stone (approximately 123 kg) while fully clothed. The limit is designed to ensure that winch systems can safely lift and transport workers to safety in the event of an emergency.

The rule applies to a range of high‑risk settings, including offshore platforms, tall‑building construction sites, and other locations where rapid evacuation is critical. By capping the maximum weight, the guideline helps maintain the integrity of winch equipment, reduces the risk of mechanical failure, and protects workers from injury during rescue operations. Employers are expected to verify compliance through pre‑deployment weight checks and to adjust protective gear or work assignments accordingly.

In summary, the 19.5‑stone weight cap is a preventive measure aimed at enhancing emergency response effectiveness. Adhering to this standard will help ensure that winch‑based rescue systems remain reliable and that workers can be safely evacuated when needed.
author: BBC Business

title: Low Gas Storage Levels Could Drive Prices Up, Experts Warn
content:
Experts have warned that the current low levels of natural‑gas storage could drive prices higher, potentially pushing up household energy bills. Analysts from the Energy Institute and several market research firms noted that storage volumes are below the 10‑year average, and that any further drawdown could tighten supply and lift spot market prices. The warning comes after a series of price spikes in the past months, which have already pushed average UK gas prices above £5 per megawatt‑hour.

The forecast comes at a time when the government is reviewing its energy‑price cap and considering additional support for vulnerable consumers. Market participants say that if storage levels do not recover before the winter, the cost of heating could rise significantly, especially for households that rely on gas boilers. While the government has pledged to monitor the situation closely, the experts suggest that without a substantial increase in storage or new supply, consumers may face higher bills in the coming months.
author: BBC Business

title: UC Berkeley Study Shows Fear Can Freeze Earthquake Response
content:
During school drills and safety briefings, most people learn to “drop, cover and hold on” when an earthquake begins.  Yet the way people actually behave in the first few seconds of shaking can be far more varied.  A team of researchers at the University of California, Berkeley is now examining those split‑second decisions, focusing on how fear and individual risk perception shape the actions people take during seismic events.

The Berkeley study uses a combination of controlled laboratory simulations and real‑time monitoring of participants in a mock‑building environment.  Subjects are exposed to realistic vibration patterns while their movements, heart rates, and verbal responses are recorded.  Researchers also administer questionnaires to gauge each participant’s perceived threat level and prior earthquake experience.  Early results indicate that higher anxiety levels correlate with more erratic movements—such as moving away from the nearest shelter or attempting to flee—rather than following the prescribed drop‑cover‑hold routine.

These findings suggest that standard safety instructions may not fully account for the psychological dynamics that influence human behavior during earthquakes.  By better understanding the link between fear, risk perception, and actual response, the team hopes to refine public education programs and emergency protocols, ultimately improving safety outcomes for communities in earthquake‑prone regions.
author: Phys.org

title: AI Tutor Improves Math Learning by Withholding Answers
content:
Schools across Canada are grappling with the rapid integration of artificial intelligence into classrooms, and new research from the University of Toronto Mississauga adds nuance to the debate. A study published this week examined the effectiveness of an AI‑driven math tutor designed to assist students while limiting direct answer provision. The findings suggest that the system can improve problem‑solving skills, but only when it deliberately withholds final solutions and instead guides learners through the reasoning process.

The research team tested the tutor with middle‑school students on a series of algebraic and geometry problems. Participants who interacted with the AI received prompts, hints, and step‑by‑step feedback rather than outright answers. Over a four‑week period, these students demonstrated higher gains in conceptual understanding and test scores compared to a control group that received standard textbook instruction. The study notes that the AI’s role as a coach—prompting reflection and encouraging exploration—appears to foster deeper engagement and persistence.

While the results highlight the potential of AI to support mathematical learning, the authors caution that the technology must be carefully calibrated to avoid simply dispensing answers. Future work will explore how best to integrate such tutors into existing curricula and assess long‑term outcomes. For educators, the study underscores that AI tools can be valuable when they promote active problem‑solving rather than passive answer retrieval.
author: Phys.org

title: Overqualified Employees' Work Priorities Increase Family Conflict, Study Finds
content:
A recent study published in the *Journal of Occupational Health Psychology* found that employees who possess higher qualifications than their current roles demand and who place work above family responsibilities are more prone to allow career‑related anxiety and fear to intrude into their domestic lives, thereby increasing interpersonal conflict at home. The research, which surveyed 1,200 professionals across the United States, revealed a statistically significant correlation between perceived job insecurity and the frequency of arguments or emotional distance reported by spouses and partners.

The authors explain that the mismatch between skill level and job expectations can generate chronic stress, which in turn manifests as irritability, reduced patience, and a tendency to bring work concerns into family conversations. “When employees feel underutilized or overqualified, the resulting frustration can spill over, eroding the quality of their home relationships,” said lead author Dr. Elena Ramirez. The study also noted that those who reported higher levels of work‑family conflict were more likely to experience symptoms of anxiety, depression, and sleep disturbances.
